author: emollick
text: What makes Claude Projects so interesting is that it handles teams of agents really well, you talk to a main orchestrator agent and it spins up specialists. Basically it creates an organization to solve your issue, mixing expensive and cheap agents depending on your preferences. For example, I asked Fable in Claude Projects to select famous historical mysteries that it could try to resolve. It initiated research agents, selected the mysteries based on data it could access, and spun up eighteen separate threads, each with an agent each focused on one mystery. Then each thread launched additional agents (simulating avalanches, breaking codes) before summarizing those and passing them to still more agents for write up and another set of skeptical agents to fact check. It did this over a day of work, with the central orchestrator agent organizing it all. The results were interesting if you like historical mysteries. They are also for fun and certainly not definitive or guaranteed error-free (but they are also mostly reasonable & grounded in the literature). https://t.co/uHToT5GNuF

author: emollick
text: I cannot emphasize enough how much GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 are already enough for transformative impact in large sections of the economy. They can reliably do weeks worth of human work when properly guided & harnessed. Those effects will not be all at once and be uneven, but the fact that change will occur is inevitable no matter how the frontier is paced. But inevitable change does not mean the type of change is inevitable. It is increasingly important that we develop & share models of AI-human work that enhance, rather than only replace, human labor. The labs have a role to play in doing this, but so do companies and industries experimenting with AI adoption, as well as policy makers who can incentivize this sort of inplemenation. This work is important regardless of existential risk, and needs a lot more focus.

author: emollick
text: What you are seeing in math right now is a consequence of the jagged frontier, and a precursor of what is to come in other professions. Yes, mathematicians do math, but they also have other tasks they view as important (mentor students, maintain a scientific community, safeguard the future of a field, foster a love of math) that AI can't do. At least one worry that mathematicians seem to have is that by focusing on the flashiest, most obvious element of what mathematicians do (make proofs), the AI companies are damaging the other tasks that AI can't do. AI can discover superhuman proofs, but that is not all that the math profession is about, and actually can undermine and reduce the attention to the other aspects of the job that are important to mathematicians. It becomes harder to defend the value of the many other tasks mathematicians do to the outside world if the most visible part is taken away. I suspect we will see more of this across fields and professions that will increasingly be forced to help people understand that their jobs consist not only the most visible tasks that AI can do, but also tasks that the AI cannot do or does badly.

author: emollick
text: An example of useful knowledge work: I assigned GPT-6 to read through tens of thousands of my emails, my writings, my calendar appointments and more to assemble a personal knowledge base of research, contacts, ideas, relationships, and tasks over my recent career. GPT-6 downloaded the appropriate software, figured out a strategy, and built a multi-gigabyte personal wiki without any further intervention from me over the course of five days of uninterrupted work. Twice a day, the AI now goes through my emails, cross-references them with this extensive knowledge base, and sends me a summary of things I should be paying attention to, things I might be interested in, etc. (Two questions you may have: Yes, I gave the AI access to my computer and this involves risks, and you should be careful before you do the same. And I do not take money from any AI lab and pay for my own usage, but during the trial period, I was not charged for tokens, so I cannot tell you how much this process would have cost, but it likely would have been very substantial. The ongoing briefings do not use substantial amounts of token)

author: emollick
text: Here are 22 more gems according to the AI among my bookmarks 1. Researchers compressed 4.1 million recipes into a two-megabyte model of human cooking. The model spans seven languages and represents 1,790 ingredients in 300 dimensions. Beyond the technical achievement, it suggests a fascinating possibility: representing entire culinary traditions as a navigable mathematical space. https://x.com/josefchen/status/2059350978109874677 2. Scientists watched a single-celled organism evolve multicellularity in real time. After researchers introduced a predator, a single-cell alga evolved into a multicellular organism. The transition reportedly took about a year—a compressed demonstration of how environmental pressure can produce a major evolutionary transition. https://x.com/SteveStuWill/status/1595570975302483968 3. The human brain contains billions of neurons but appears to process conscious thought at roughly ten bits per second. This paper asks why our enormous biological machinery produces such a narrow stream of conscious processing—and why we can generally think about only one thing at a time. https://x.com/EricTopol/status/1869054294735085714 4. Leaded gasoline may have reduced the cognitive ability of about half the American population. A study estimated the population-scale impact of childhood lead exposure from automobile exhaust. It is a remarkable example of a mundane technology quietly imposing enormous social costs. https://x.com/NBCNews/status/1501049339321499648 5. Cats may exploit change blindness to sneak up on us. Change blindness is our failure to notice even dramatic environmental changes while our attention is elsewhere. This post connects the phenomenon to a familiar feline behavior: moving closer whenever you look away. https://x.com/DegenRolf/status/1363372173017157641 6. When did modern civilization finally surpass the technological achievements of the ancient world? The answer was far less obvious to people living in 1599 or even 1715 than it seems today. This essay reconstructs how early-modern thinkers assessed their own technology relative to antiquity. https://x.com/antonhowes/status/1722939185961607511 7. People in nearly every generation believe that morality is declining. Even young people often believe that today’s generation is worse than those that came before it. Research on the “illusion of moral decline” suggests that this recurring perception is produced by predictable biases in memory and attention. https://x.com/alexolegimas/status/2004593132508512724 8. Here is a recreation of an entire GPT architecture inside a spreadsheet. It is a working nanoGPT with approximately 85,000 parameters, small enough to fit inside a spreadsheet file. Because the data and parameters are visible, it turns an otherwise opaque transformer model into something you can inspect cell by cell. https://x.com/chendabo/status/1799614807878095359 9. Studying the brain’s hardware may not explain human intelligence any more than studying computer hardware explains Excel pivot tables. This paper argues that human intelligence cannot be understood independently of accumulated culture. Much of what makes an individual capable exists outside the individual—in tools, institutions, norms, and knowledge inherited from other people. https://x.com/mmuthukrishna/status/1684576118370967552 10. When AI became better than humans at Go, human players subsequently became better too. Professional Go players began learning from strategies discovered by machines, producing an unusual example of superhuman AI expanding rather than simply replacing human capability. https://x.com/emollick/status/1508651631151362050 11. The familiar integer values assigned to chess pieces are convenient—but not really correct. A pawn is worth one, a bishop or knight roughly three, and a rook five. But a game as contextual as chess should not yield perfectly tidy integer values. This thread investigates what the pieces are actually worth. https://x.com/martinmbauer/status/1624329951200649217 12. There is film of Paul McCartney going from almost nothing to the beginnings of a hit song in roughly 45 seconds. It is a rare chance to watch creative expertise operating in real time: not merely performing or explaining a finished work, but discovering it. https://x.com/tedgioia/status/1465049482933030913 13. What if The Lord of the Rings had emerged from ancient China? An artist reimagined Frodo and the Fellowship through the visual language of ancient China. It is not merely a costume swap; it demonstrates how strongly world-building depends on an underlying cultural vocabulary. https://x.com/leiahamart/status/1478106554268192772 14. Why does the post-scarcity civilization in Iain M. Banks’s Culture novels remain so compelling? “Why the Culture Wins” examines the political and philosophical appeal of Banks’s civilization—and why it feels like more than a conventional science-fiction utopia. https://x.com/tszzl/status/1713307250574696645 15. The University of Chicago offers a four-year Great Books discussion course that is open to anyone. The program provides a structured route through foundational works without requiring enrollment in a degree. Andy Matuschak completed its first year and shared his observations. https://x.com/andy_matuschak/status/1662181844488720384 16. A collection of rules that produced exactly the opposite of their intended effects. One example: banning alcohol inside college football stadiums led fans to drink more beforehand, increasing intoxication problems. The thread collects similar cases in which incentives and adaptation defeated seemingly sensible policies. https://x.com/TrungTPhan/status/1311300651645767682 17. Here are 29 slides explaining the plot of Tenet. The post is funny, but it is also an impressive exercise in visual explanation: taking a deliberately disorienting film about inverted time and attempting to make its causal structure comprehensible. https://x.com/jasonjoyride/status/1743316835972546580 18. This graphic compares how quickly every planet rotates—and the direction each one points. Jupiter spins at a remarkable speed, while Venus barely turns at all and rotates in the opposite direction from most planets. It makes the solar system feel less like a tidy diagram and more like a collection of wildly different physical worlds. https://x.com/Cmdr_Hadfield/status/1795168715568201909 19. Mario games demonstrate that two mechanically similar experiences can feel psychologically different. The example is a compact lesson in design: objective similarity does not produce subjective equivalence. Presentation, framing, feedback, and context can transform how the same underlying structure feels. https://x.com/Cheesemeister3k/status/1547440825420099586 20. An AI learned to defeat elite human poker players in a game of hidden information. Unlike chess or Go, poker requires reasoning about uncertainty, deception, and opponents who know things you do not. Pluribus decisively beat five professionals across 10,000 hands, making it an unusually important—and still underappreciated—AI result. https://x.com/deedydas/status/1875206105825165494 21. An open-source tool can turn any city into a minimalist map poster. Choose a place and generate a clean, highly detailed visual from its street network. It is a lovely example of public geographic data becoming personal art. https://x.com/geerlingguy/status/2012666150379716969 22. A mostly complete visual map of neural-network architectures. The field contains far more varieties than the phrase “neural network” suggests. This graphic organizes many of them into a single taxonomy, making decades of architectural experimentation visible at once. https://x.com/hamptonism/status/1806279209351782612

author: emollick
text: Here are the gems the AI picked: 1. Sperm whales may have collectively learned how to evade whalers. Within a few years, the success rate of whalers’ harpoons reportedly fell by 58%, suggesting that information about the attacks was being shared among whales. An astonishing example of nonhuman culture adapting under pressure. https://x.com/SteveStuWill/status/1475711589374377985 2. A 500,000–300,000-year-old handaxe was deliberately crafted around a fossil shell. The shell sits near the center of the tool, raising the possibility that its maker noticed and intentionally incorporated it. It may represent a startlingly early form of aesthetic intention. https://x.com/AlisonFisk/status/1776921375980024090 3. Intelligence may be far more distributed throughout biology than we generally recognize. This thread explores Michael Levin’s work on the underappreciated collective intelligence of cells and biological systems—and the perspective shifts that follow if we stop treating intelligence as something that happens only inside brains. https://x.com/kasratweets/status/1783217644897984636 4. Wikipedia succeeded while seven similar online encyclopedia projects failed. They appeared at roughly the same time and pursued similar goals, but only one became a foundational part of the internet. This paper looks for the institutional and organizational reasons why. https://x.com/OwainEvans_UK/status/1329892507325509640 5. Beautiful data visualizations are more likely to be trusted. Across four studies, people placed more trust in more aesthetically pleasing graphs—even when beauty shouldn’t have affected the credibility of the underlying information. A useful warning for anyone who creates or consumes research. https://x.com/Mark_A_Thornton/status/1478057342088495112 6. Choosing the right problem may be the highest-leverage skill in research. This long thread and accompanying Cell article examine how scientists and engineers select problems, including practical decision trees for deciding what is actually worth pursuing. https://x.com/mfgrp/status/1778440273988812835 7. One man spent five years recreating all 107 recipes in the Alinea cookbook. What begins as a story of culinary obsession becomes a lesson about mastery, deliberate practice, and the strange process by which a consumer becomes a creator. https://x.com/kevinleeme/status/1284184707110809600 8. Shortly after World War I began, the Financial Times asked readers to predict how the war would change the map of Europe. It was presented as a game. There were cash prizes. It is a deeply strange and revealing artifact of how people perceived a catastrophe before its true scale was understood. https://x.com/khalafroula/status/2022949964234535159 9. Charles Darwin once received a scientific critique of On the Origin of Species—and wrote a remarkable reply. Julia Galef explains why it may be her favorite letter in the history of science and what it reveals about Darwin’s intellectual character. https://x.com/juliagalef/status/1341058267175378950 10. Dungeons & Dragons contains technical debt inherited from its earliest origins. Its time and distance scales never quite synchronized because of rules inherited from the miniature-wargame Chainmail. That mismatch may also help explain why modern D&D characters feel like superheroes. https://x.com/mikemearls/status/1878466880098242688 11. Avant-garde perfume is an accessible form of experimental art. There is an entire world of strange, conceptual, independently produced perfume—and samples are inexpensive enough that it may be one of the easiest ways to explore a completely unfamiliar aesthetic medium. https://x.com/add_hawk/status/1357071738731814912 12. ShadeMap simulates every mountain, building, and tree shadow in the world. You can choose any location, date, and time and see how sunlight and shadow move across the landscape. It is both practically useful and oddly mesmerizing. https://x.com/shademap/status/1796244182417424670 13. The Whole Earth Index is a nearly complete, freely accessible archive of Whole Earth publications. The Whole Earth Catalog was one of the most influential documents of the counterculture and early technological imagination. Now much of that world is searchable online. https://x.com/longnow/status/1712877725353234442 14. One project explored all 54 African countries through 54 works of architecture. Each project was intended to reflect the cultural identity and history of a different nation, creating an unusually ambitious visual survey of African architecture and design. https://x.com/omar_degan/status/1347485800062201858 15. Infinite Craft is an endless game of combinatorial discovery. You begin with a few basic elements and combine them to create new concepts, which can then be combined again. It is a wonderfully compact demonstration of how generative systems can produce genuine exploration and surprise. https://x.com/nealagarwal/status/1752716375255101440

author: erikbryn
text: RT by @emollick: .@BharatKChandar, @RuyuChen and I just released an updated version of our paper "Canaries in the Coal Mine?" The headline is that we still don't see any widespread job displacement due to AI, but the earlier trends we identified hold up or even grow. E.g., the relative decline for young people in AI-exposed jobs widened to 19% by June 2026, from 15% in our first wave. We also looked at changes in interest rates, remote work, the tech sector boom and bust and remote work, but none of them seem to explain the effects we see for AI-exposed jobs. Bharat has a great thread below with more detial. It ends with links to the new paper and to a short blog post summarizing what's new. I'd love to hear what you think.

author: emollick
text: A true issue with data centers compared with the light industries of previous Industrial Revolutions is they don’t require many people to run (though building them takes more). It breaks the industry trade-offs between palpable local negative externalities & palpable local gains.

author: emollick
text: Has been any published data or studies that would support either of the two sides: “the way to stop cyberattacks from advanced AI is to give everyone advanced AI at once” vs “the way to stop cyberattacks from advanced AI is to limit access to only key firms for a long period”?

author: emollick

author: emollick
text: Spark is the big news and is a good model. Not quite at the frontier of open models from China, and still well behind the closed frontier, but the best non-Chinese open weights model released in a year. Of course, a lot depends on continuing to release new open models to keep up

author: emollick
text: Big Tech should have either kept calling them server farms (agricultural, quaint) or started calling them supercomputing facilities (futuristic, exciting). Data centers (why my data? why is it centralized?) was the worst possible choice.

author: emollick
text: I feel like the debate over AI in academic journals is way too focused on where the capabilities of AI are today (or even where they were a couple years ago) and not nearly focused on where they will almost certainly be in the coming years… … and publication takes many years.

author: emollick

author: emollick
text: In general, the potential of LLMs to make older work more accessible is underrated. That can be helping people experience forms of media that are now obsolete or hard-to-use. It can also be creating interpretative or context bridges between older work and today.

author: emollick
text: A thing that people don't get about academia is that we have a whole bunch of parallel fights about academic stuff (ranging from high-minded philosophical debates to petty rivalries about credit) that spill over into X in ways that are non-obvious to those outside a given field.

author: emollick
text: Is all code becoming the same? On one hand, 95% of Kaggle submissions that set a random seed now use 42 (a Hitchhiker's Guide joke LLMs love). But, it turns out that while coding syntax is converging, approaches to problems are not converging. Human prompters drive real variety.

author: emollick
text: It is not a novel observation at this point, but the collapse of Google’s Gemini as a frontier model series is still astonishing. Unlike Meta & SpaceX, Google has captive Gemini customers at an enterprise level, so the fact that they are pushed towards Gemini 3.1 Pro is a problem

author: emollick
text: It is past time to take AI & security seriously at the individual level as well. If its not the current OpenAI and Anthropic models doing it, then the coming open weights models will when they catch up. Assume if things can be found on the open internet, they will be found.
